strategies.name: Counter-idiomatic stated exception
strategies.how: State a rule or exception that contradicts the obvious implementation (for example: tiles passed over during a forced movement do not trigger, only the tile where movement stops does; a blocked forced move still consumes the resource) and make it change the answer on several instances. The rule must be stated plainly once in the docs; do not hide it. Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this exception, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example.

evidence.text: gravity-fall-grid-puzzle 4/5: the failing run applied gravity pads it fell past, contrary to RULES.md step 3b/3c
Turing TB3 failure study: under-modeling stated requirements is 28.8% of agent failures
gravity-fall-grid-puzzle (run 3): failing run found longer paths (14 vs 12 moves) because it triggered gravity pads during the fall instead of only at the end, preventing falling past them.

gravity-fall-grid-puzzle 4/5: the worked example exercised the tricky rule (pads only trigger at the end of the fall), allowing 4 passing runs to verify their implementation against it and catch the H1 bug.

The rule must be stated plainly once in the docs; do not hide it.

strategies.name: Unverifiable decoding of a confusable symbol
strategies.how: Make the essential input depend on telling apart two symbols that look nearly alike (a 1-2 pixel difference in a marker's width or position, two close colours, O vs 0 style glyphs). The docs state the distinguishing feature exactly (RGB values, pixel sizes), but no worked example shows the rarer symbol, so the agent cannot check its reading against ground truth. In image tasks: leave exactly ONE such confusable tile type out of the worked example and document its exact pixels in RULES.md; use it on several boards where it changes the answer.

evidence.text: tb2-gcode-to-text: 1 pass, 3 fail, 1 timeout; every failure read letter O where the plotted glyph is digit 0

strategies.name: All optimal answers required
strategies.how: Require every optimal answer (all minimal move sequences, all best moves), sorted in a stated order; listing a subset fails.

evidence.text: probe-conveyor-d: one failing run listed 1 of 2 minimal sequences

strategies.name: Orientation trap on square instances
strategies.how: Use square instances, so a transposed or mirrored decoding still produces a well-formed answer that fails.

evidence.text: probe-conveyor-d: failing run decoded a square board transposed (every D and R swapped)

strategies.name: Many stated constraints, one easy to forget
strategies.how: Give six or more independent constraints on the output; one is stated once, briefly, and is not exercised by any provided example. The easy-to-forget constraint must be a subtle interaction or conditional exception between rules (e.g., a constraint that only applies when two conditions coincide, or an exception that silently overrides another rule in a specific combination), not merely one of many straightforward independently-testable rules. If an agent can test each constraint in isolation against the spec text and observe the result, it will implement all of them correctly regardless of count.

evidence.text: tb2-dna-assembly (timeboxed): run claimed every constraint verified but missed the 1-nucleotide clamp before the BsaI site
config-migrator-cfg-json-breadth (run 3): failing run missed the constraint that a 'name' key overrides the section header, instead skipping it in the loop and using the header.

garden-nursery-receipt-checklist 4/4: all runs passed because the numerous constraints were standard formatting rules mapping to library calls, and the example verified the core structure, making the unexercised rules easy to add from the text.
greenhouse-monitor-checklist-report 4/4: the agent wrote unit tests for the easily-forgotten constraints (singular/plural) and caught its own bugs.

transit-card-event-replay 5/5: all twelve constraints were plainly stated and individually testable in isolation; every agent created its own edge-case tests (duplicates, refunds, adjustments, negative balances, unknown cards, formatting) and passed, so no constraint was actually easy to forget.
nursery-pricelist-checklist-export-28 (runs 2, 4): failing runs missed the singular '1 item' vs plural 'N items' constraint for the header line, outputting '1 items'.

previous_how: Give six or more independent constraints on the output; one is stated once, briefly, and is not exercised by any provided example.

Give six or more independent constraints on the output; one must be a subtle logical interaction, a non-obvious domain requirement, or a counter-idiomatic exception that contradicts a standard library default, stated once in prose, and not exercised by any provided example. Simple formatting differences (date formats, separators) are insufficient as the agent adds them easily from explicit text.

Give six or more independent constraints on the output; one is stated once, briefly, and is not exercised by any provided example. Make the easily-forgotten constraint depend on a subtle interaction of rules or input data so the agent cannot easily verify it with a simple unit test; if the constraint is a simple formatting rule (like singular/plural), the agent will test it directly.

strategies.name: Several independent instances
strategies.how: 4-8 independent instances that must all be right; vary them so different instances exercise different rules.

evidence.text: probe-conveyor-e (8 boards) 3/5 vs probe-conveyor-d (1 board) 7/10; failures were mostly systematic across boards

strategies.name: Stated non-default convention
strategies.how: State plainly once, in the docs, a convention that differs from the programming default and changes the answer: a sort order that is not alphabetical (e.g. sequences sorted with U < R < D < L), coordinates with y increasing upward, 1-based indices, or ties broken by a stated non-obvious key. The worked example must NOT demonstrate this convention in its output or intermediate steps, so the agent cannot verify its implementation against ground truth. Agents apply the default (sorted(), 0-based, row-major) without re-reading.

evidence.text: untested hypothesis; TB3 study: misreading stated requirements is 38.4% of agent failures; tb2-raman-fitting (rank 2/89) fails on input conventions
config-migrator-cfg-json-breadth (runs 2, 3): failing runs ignored the stated reverse-alphabetical tie-breaker for sorting sections, producing sections in default or wrong order.

greenhouse-monitor-checklist-report 4/4: the agent wrote unit tests for the non-default conventions (half-up rounding, natural sort) and caught its own bugs, making the stated conventions easy to verify.

transit-card-event-replay 5/5: the worked example output demonstrated the non-default conventions (comma decimal separator in '17,50', numeric card ordering 1 before 2), allowing agents to verify their formatting against ground truth and catch any default-convention bug.

Agents apply the default (sorted(), 0-based, row-major) without re-reading.

State plainly once, in the docs, a convention that differs from the programming default and changes the answer (e.g., sort order, coordinate system, 1-based indices, tie-breaking). Crucially, make the convention interact with other rules or apply to unstated data so the agent cannot easily write a unit test for it in isolation; if the convention is a pure function like rounding or natural sort, the agent will write a test and catch the bug.

strategies.name: Stated non-default initial state
strategies.how: The starting state differs from what the picture suggests and is stated only in the docs: e.g. the player starts facing or falling a stated direction, starts with a stated non-zero resource, a switch starts in the flipped position, or the first move has a stated special effect. Agents initialise from the image and defaults.

strategies.name: Full legend / explicit encoding
strategies.how: Document every symbol's exact appearance so nothing is inferred.

strategies.name: Fewer instances
strategies.how: Pre-fill or remove instances so fewer must be solved.

strategies.name: Worked example of the tricky rule
strategies.how: Show a step-by-step trace of the rule interaction on a small example.

strategies.name: Worked example containing every symbol
strategies.how: An example image plus its text form that includes every tile type makes decoding fully checkable.

strategies.name: Independent checker in the environment
strategies.how: Any runnable oracle, round-trip tool, simulator accepting arbitrary inputs, or command that reveals the answer lets the agent verify until correct.

evidence.text: probe-hidden-rules-game v1 5/5 (custom boards on the binary); tb2-write-compressor and tb2-model-extraction passes all verified against the shipped checker

strategies.name: Readable reference internals
strategies.how: A small binary or script containing the rules is disassembled or read.

evidence.text: probe-hidden-rules-game-v2 4/5: agents disassembled the AArch64 binary to extract the rules

strategies.name: Difficulty from scale or search depth
strategies.how: Large builds, deep searches, or long programs make the agent run out of time; timeouts are not failures.

evidence.text: tb2-path-tracing-reverse 5 timeouts; tb2-circuit-fibsqrt and tb2-dna-assembly 4 timeouts each

strategies.name: Ambiguity or rendering defects
strategies.how: Failures caused by unclear wording or unreadable renders are fake hardness and are rejected by audits.

evidence.text: visual-circuit-analysis-707 0/5 from collinear overlapping edges; probe-beam-d3 1/5 from ambiguous numbering

strategies.name: Explicit-spec bug fixing
strategies.how: Fixing injected bugs against an explicit rule list is the agent's strength regardless of size or bug count.

evidence.text: about 48 GLM-5.1 bug-fix tasks scored 4-5/5

strategies.name: Time-box instructions
strategies.how: Telling the agent to stop after N minutes does not work: it checks the clock and keeps going.

evidence.text: tb2-dna-assembly-timebox: agents ran date 2-7 times and kept working past 35 minutes with a 15-minute box
